notes:
I found good material for verses 23, 25–27, 31 and 32–43. I couldn't find anything for verses 24, 28, 29 and 30, so those are left out. Nothing turned up from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, the Catholic sites, the Lutheran or Wesleyan sites, or on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching for this passage.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 23**
- Precept Austin points out that "proclaim" (v. 20) and "confounding" (v. 22) are both in the Greek imperfect tense. Saul kept preaching, the Jews grew more and more confused, and the greater their opposition grew as shown by their reaction in Acts 9:23. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary
- Lowell Johnson places "many days" in a section titled "In Arabia – God used Solitude Acts 9:20-23". That links this verse to Paul's time in Arabia (Gal 1). https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-acts-lowell-johnson
- Ellicott (quoted in the notes on v. 43) says that in Acts 9:23, as we have seen, the words covered a period of nearly three years. The Pulpit Commentary calls the same phrase a time of indeterminate length. https://biblehub.com/acts/9-43.htm

**v. 25**
- A. T. Robertson notes that Damascus may have been under Aretas of Arabia as it certainly was a couple of years later when Saul escaped in a basket (2 Corinthians 11:32). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rwp/acts-9.html

**v. 26**
- John Phillips (quoted by Precept Austin) says the believers all avoided Saul, naturally thinking he had come to spy on them. He also asks why Peter, John or Andrew didn't reach out to him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary

**v. 27**
- A. T. Robertson says Barnabas had the insight and the courage to stand by Saul at the crucial moment in his life when the evidence seemed to be against him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary
- Precept Austin's own comment: Ananias and Barnabas are two witnesses that Saul really saw the risen Jesus. Seeing Him met a major criteria of a genuine NT apostle. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-9-commentary

**v. 31**
- Lowell Johnson calls the verse a summary of the early church's condition and growth, showing a godly balance in the early church. Note two words: Edified and Multiplied. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-acts-lowell-johnson

**v. 32**
- David Guzik (Enduring Word) says the earlier pattern changed. Instead of people coming to the apostles in Jerusalem, Peter now went out, traveling about 35 miles to Lydda. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- Bob Utley (bible.org) thinks Peter was apparently revisiting churches Philip had started. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-9

**v. 33**
- Opinions differ on whether Aeneas was already a believer:
  - Robertson thinks he was probably a Hellenistic Jew and apparently a disciple already (the saint, verse Acts 9:32). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rwp/acts-9.html
  - Utley says it is uncertain whether he was a believer. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-9

**v. 34**
- Guzik: Peter clearly named the healer. Peter was only His instrument. Jesus healed with the power of Jesus, but Peter did not heal with the power of Peter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- R. C. Sproul notes the phrase could be translated "Jesus the Christ is healing you"—that is, at that moment. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/raising-dorcas
- Alexander Maclaren sees Peter deliberately copying his Master's healing of the paralytic ("Arise, and make thy bed"). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-34.htm
- Gill reads the words as a declaration that Christ's healing power was at work right then, not as a prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-34.htm

**v. 35**
- Steven Cole (bible.org) says "all" probably does not mean every single person, but rather, a great number. He also notes that Luke states the miracles' purpose twice, here and in v. 42. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-24-faith-god-all-power-acts-932-43

**v. 36**
- **Her names:** Both names mean "gazelle" or "deer." Ellicott says bearing both names suggests ties to both the Hebrew-speaking and Greek-speaking parts of the church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-36.htm
- **"Disciple":** Vincent notes that the word is a feminine form only here in New Testament. The Cambridge Bible says she is called a disciple to show there is no male-or-female distinction under the gospel (Gal 3:28). The Pulpit Commentary mentions that some think she was a deaconess of the Church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-36.htm
- **"Which she did":** Guzik says Luke added these words because some people are full of good works only in their minds, while Tabitha actually did them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/

**v. 37**
- Utley: The washing of the body was typical of the Jewish preparation for burial. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-9
- Matthew Henry thinks they didn't bury her because they hoped Peter would raise her. He also suggests the washing showed she was truly dead. Lightfoot (as cited by Henry) thinks the upper room may have been the believers' meeting room. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-40.html

**v. 38**
- Most think they hoped Peter would raise her:
  - Thomas Constable says they apparently expected Peter to raise her, since they washed her body and laid it out instead of burying it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-38.html
  - GotQuestions is more careful: the Bible doesn't say they hoped for that, only that they called for him urgently. https://www.gotquestions.org/Dorcas-in-the-Bible.html
  - Guzik thinks they may have hoped only for comfort. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/

**v. 39**
- Utley thinks the widows were apparently wearing the inner and outer garments Dorcas had made for them. https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-9

**v. 40**
- **The parallel with Jesus:** Guzik notes Jesus said "Talitha, cumi" (Mark 5), and Peter said "Tabitha cumi." Peter was simply doing what Jesus did. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/ Maclaren adds that the words differ by only one letter, and that Peter did something Christ didn't do: he prayed first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-34.htm
- **Prayer before the command:** John MacArthur is glad it doesn't say Peter simply knelt and spoke the command. Peter prayed and acknowledged where the power came from. https://www.gty.org/sermons/print/1733/marks-of-an-effective-personal-ministry-part-2
- **Raised, not resurrected:** Guzik stresses that Dorcas was not *resurrected*; she was *resuscitated* to her old life, where she would die again. He adds that God raised her while Stephen and James stayed dead, which shows God's ways are beyond our knowing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/

**v. 41**
- Matthew Henry: she sat up to show she was truly alive. By giving her his hand, Peter welcomed her back to life and gave her the right hand of fellowship among the living. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-40.html

**v. 42**
- Henry: Joppa was a seaport, so the news would travel abroad quickly. This was the design of miracles, to confirm a divine revelation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-40.html
- The Geneva Study Bible says that by raising the dead through Christ's name, Peter shows he preaches the glad tidings of life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-36.htm

**v. 43**
- **A step toward Acts 10:** Many writers agree that tanning was seen as unclean work, so staying with Simon marked a step forward for Peter:
  - Ellicott says Peter was taking a step toward greater freedom and being trained for fuller understanding. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-43.htm
  - Guzik says this prepared the ground for the next chapter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- **A caution:** The Pulpit Commentary says it would not be safe to conclude that Peter already ignored ceremonial uncleanness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-43.htm
- **Humility:** Matthew Henry says Peter didn't stay with the well-off Tabitha but with an ordinary tradesman, as an example of humility (Rom 12:16). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-43.html

## 2. Where traditions differ

The sites don't frame any of these as formal denominational disputes. The clearest difference is over whether miracles like these still happen today (vv. 34, 40).
- **John MacArthur (Grace to You, Baptist-leaning):** God worked these miracles through His apostles. He cites 2 Corinthians 12:12, where wonders and mighty deeds are called the signs of an apostle. https://www.gty.org/sermons/print/1733/marks-of-an-effective-personal-ministry-part-2
- **David Guzik (Calvary Chapel):** Such miracles have happened and still do, though one is wise not to gullibly accept every reported instance of such. Nothing in Acts suggests Christians expected the dead to be raised as a matter of course. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-9/
- **Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel):** The dynamic power of the Holy Spirit is one of the marks of the early church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/9-40.html
- **R. C. Sproul (Reformed):** He uses the healing to point to our hope. Jesus is making us whole now, but no one of us is whole yet, though we will be someday. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/raising-dorcas
- **Steven Cole (bible.org, evangelical):** As far as he knows, the New Testament has no examples of believers being miraculously healed, though three were raised from the dead. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-24-faith-god-all-power-acts-932-43

## 3. Other views

**v. 36 (Orthodox):** The Orthodox Church in America honors her as "Saint Tabitha the Widow." It describes her as a virtuous member of the Joppa church, and says Peter prayed on bended knee after arriving to find her already dead. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/1952/10/25/103058-saint-tabitha-the-widow-raised-from-the-dead-by-the-apostle-pete By contrast, Robertson thinks she was probably unmarried, since no husband is mentioned. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rwp/acts-9.html

**v. 43 (Church Fathers):** The Expositor's Greek Testament says Chrysostom and Theophylact both use this verse to show Peter's unassuming conduct. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/9-43.htm
